prompt: Which experiment most cleanly tests the effect of concentration alone on reaction rate?
options: Using 1 mol/L acid at 20 °C and 2 mol/L acid at 40 °C with the same marble chips
Using 1 mol/L acid and 2 mol/L acid at the same temperature, with the same mass and particle size of marble chips
Using the same concentration of acid but changing the temperature each time
Using powder in one experiment and chips in another with the same concentration
explanation: To isolate concentration as the variable, every other factor (temperature, surface area, mass of solid) must be kept the same — the fair test changes only the acid concentration.
hint: A fair test changes only ONE variable — which option only changes concentration and keeps everything else the same?

prompt: A student correctly argues that stirring a reaction mixture does NOT qualify as a separate factor affecting rate. Which reasoning best supports this view?
options: Stirring reduces temperature by convection, so it is really a temperature effect

Stirring keeps the concentration uniform throughout the mixture and can expose fresh solid surface — its effect is accounted for by concentration and surface area; stirring is not a distinct physical cause of rate change
Stirring is never observed to change reaction rate under any circumstances
Stirring is a separate factor but only matters in reactions involving gases
explanation: Stirring prevents local depletion of reactants near the solid surface (keeping effective concentration high) and may chip off spent surface (exposing fresh surface area); both effects are explained by concentration and surface area, so stirring is not an independent factor.
hint: Think about what stirring actually does physically — does it change concentration or surface area, or is it something entirely new?

prompt: A student claims: 'A bigger lump of calcium carbonate has more surface area than a small piece because it is bigger.' Why is this reasoning flawed in the context of reaction rates?
options: No flaw — larger lumps always react faster because they contain more material
The flaw is that calcium carbonate reacts faster in larger lumps due to internal pressure
The flaw is that a large lump has a smaller SURFACE AREA TO MASS ratio than the same mass divided into small pieces; rate depends on area per gram, not total lump size
The flaw is that smaller pieces are actually heavier per cubic centimetre
explanation: While a larger lump has more surface area than a single tiny chip of the same shape, the same MASS divided into many small pieces has far greater total surface area — and surface area per gram is what determines the rate, not the absolute size of one piece.
hint: Compare the total surface area of one big cube with the total surface area of the same mass of material divided into many tiny cubes — which is larger?

prompt: A 1 cm cube of calcium carbonate is cut into 1 mm cubes. By what factor does the total surface area increase?
options: 2 times
5 times
10 times
100 times
explanation: A 1 cm cube has side 10 mm, so it can be cut into 10³ = 1000 small cubes. Each 1 mm cube has surface area 6 × (1 mm)² = 6 mm². Total = 6000 mm². Original cube surface area = 6 × (10 mm)² = 600 mm². Ratio = 6000/600 = 10 times greater.
hint: Work out the surface area of one 1 cm cube, then calculate the total surface area of all the 1 mm cubes made from it.

prompt: Two experiments use 0.5 g of calcium carbonate with excess acid. Experiment P uses one large chip; Experiment Q uses finely ground powder. Which statement is accurate?
options: Q finishes faster AND produces more CO₂ than P
P finishes faster because the large chip traps CO₂ inside
Both P and Q produce the same total volume of CO₂, but Q finishes faster
P produces more CO₂ because the chip maintains contact with acid longer
explanation: Both use 0.5 g of CaCO₃ with excess acid, so the same number of moles react in both experiments — yielding the same total CO₂. The powder simply reaches that total faster due to higher surface area.
hint: The total CO₂ is set by how many moles of CaCO₃ you start with — surface area only changes how quickly that CO₂ is produced.

prompt: A student compares powder vs chips experiments (same mass CaCO₃, excess acid). Both finish; the powder finishes sooner. They then add more acid to both after the reaction stops. What would happen?
options: Both would produce more gas because the extra acid increases concentration
Only the powder flask would produce more gas because it reacted faster before
Neither would produce more gas — the CaCO₃ is used up; adding more acid cannot make more gas without more CaCO₃
The chips flask would now catch up and produce gas at the same rate as the powder
explanation: Both flasks used excess acid originally but the same 0.5 g of CaCO₃ was the limiting reagent; once all the CaCO₃ is consumed, adding more acid has no reactant left to react with — no further gas is produced.
hint: Which reactant was fully consumed in both experiments? Once that is gone, can adding more of the other reactant produce more product?

prompt: A student compares: (A) CaCO₃ chips + 1 mol/L HCl at 20 °C vs (B) CaCO₃ powder + 0.5 mol/L HCl at 40 °C. Can this test reveal whether surface area or temperature has a bigger effect?
options: Yes — whichever is faster proves which factor is more important
No — two variables changed simultaneously (surface area AND temperature AND concentration), so it is impossible to attribute any rate difference to a single factor
Yes — temperature always dominates so the result tells us temperature wins
No — neither surface area nor temperature affects rate, so the experiment is pointless
explanation: A valid comparison requires changing only one variable at a time (fair test). Here, surface area, temperature, AND concentration all differ between A and B; any rate difference cannot be attributed to just one factor.
hint: How many things are different between Experiment A and Experiment B — and what does that mean for drawing conclusions?

prompt: A scientist doubles the surface area of a solid reactant while halving the concentration of the dissolved acid (same temperature). Predict the overall effect on initial reaction rate.
options: Rate increases overall because surface area always wins
Rate decreases overall because concentration always wins
Rate remains approximately unchanged — doubling surface area and halving concentration have roughly opposing effects on collision frequency
Rate doubles because the two effects add together
explanation: Doubling surface area approximately doubles the number of solid particles available for collisions; halving the concentration approximately halves the acid particles reaching each surface site. These two effects roughly cancel, leaving the overall rate similar.
hint: Think about what doubling surface area does to collisions, and what halving concentration does — do they work in opposite directions?

prompt: A student tests reaction rate at three concentrations: 0.5, 1.0, and 2.0 mol/L HCl with the same marble chips at 25 °C. The rate values are approximately 0.4, 0.8, and 1.6 cm³/s. What relationship does this show?
options: Rate is inversely proportional to concentration
Rate is proportional to the square of concentration
Rate is directly proportional to concentration — doubling concentration doubles the rate
Rate increases but not proportionally — it levels off at high concentration
explanation: 0.5 → 1.0 mol/L (×2 concentration) gives 0.4 → 0.8 cm³/s (×2 rate); 1.0 → 2.0 mol/L (×2) gives 0.8 → 1.6 cm³/s (×2 rate). This is direct proportionality: rate ∝ [HCl].
hint: Compare the concentration ratios and the rate ratios at each step — do they match each other?

prompt: Three students each try a different approach to speed up a reaction: Student A raises the temperature; Student B uses powdered chalk instead of chips; Student C uses more concentrated acid. Whose approach increases BOTH collision frequency AND collision energy?
options: Student A only
Student B only
Student C only
Students B and C equally
explanation: Raising temperature (Student A) increases particle kinetic energy, boosting both collision frequency (faster-moving particles) AND collision energy (more energetic impacts). Concentration (C) and surface area (B) increase frequency but not the energy of individual collisions.
hint: Which factor gives particles more kinetic energy per particle — making each collision more energetic — rather than just making collisions more numerous?

prompt: A student plans three trials: (1) marble chips, 20 °C, 1 mol/L acid; (2) marble powder, 30 °C, 2 mol/L acid; (3) marble powder, 20 °C, 1 mol/L acid. They claim 'Trial 3 vs Trial 1 tests surface area.' Is this correct?
options: Yes — Trial 3 vs Trial 1 changes only the particle size, so it fairly tests surface area
No — Trial 3 vs Trial 1 also changes temperature and concentration, so it is not a fair test of surface area
Yes — any comparison involving powder tests surface area regardless of other variables
No — Trial 3 vs Trial 1 changes nothing; both are identical
explanation: Trial 1 (chips, 20 °C, 1 mol/L) vs Trial 3 (powder, 20 °C, 1 mol/L) changes only particle size (surface area), with temperature and concentration held constant — this is a valid fair test of surface area.
hint: Compare the conditions of Trial 1 and Trial 3 carefully — how many variables differ between them?

prompt: A student investigates the catalytic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide. She varies the mass of MnO₂ added (0.1 g, 0.5 g, 1.0 g) while keeping the volume and concentration of H₂O₂ the same. Which result would she most likely observe?
options: More MnO₂ increases the rate of oxygen production but the final volume of O₂ is the same in all three
More MnO₂ increases the final volume of oxygen collected
More MnO₂ decreases the rate because it blocks the surface of the solution
The mass of MnO₂ has no effect on either the rate or the final volume
explanation: More catalyst provides more catalytic surface, so the rate increases with more MnO₂. However, total O₂ depends only on the amount of H₂O₂ — the same in all three — so final volume is identical.
hint: More catalyst → faster, but the total O₂ still depends on the amount of ___.

prompt: A catalytic converter in a car uses platinum to convert CO and NO into CO₂ and N₂. After 10 years of use, analysis shows platinum is still present in the converter. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Platinum is consistent with behaving as a catalyst, since it is not consumed in the reaction
Platinum was not actually involved in the reactions
Platinum has been continuously replaced by the manufacturer
Platinum was slowly produced as a by-product of combustion
explanation: Finding platinum unchanged after millions of reaction cycles is exactly what we expect of a catalyst — it is not consumed. This confirms its catalytic role.
hint: What property of a catalyst allows it to be used over and over again?

prompt: The graph of oxygen volume vs. time for hydrogen peroxide decomposition with a small amount of MnO₂ shows a curve that is steep at first, then levels off. A second experiment uses the same amount of H₂O₂ but twice as much MnO₂. Which description matches the second curve?
options: Steeper initially, levels off at twice the final volume
Same steepness initially, same final volume
Less steep initially, levels off at a lower final volume
Steeper initially, levels off at the same final volume but sooner
explanation: More catalyst → faster initial rate → steeper curve. But the same amount of H₂O₂ is used, so the same total O₂ is produced — the curve just reaches that level sooner.
hint: More catalyst means the reaction is faster, but does the amount of H₂O₂ change?

prompt: Yeast contains enzymes that convert glucose into ethanol and CO₂ during brewing. A brewer doubles the amount of yeast used but keeps the glucose solution the same. What is the most likely outcome?
options: Twice as much ethanol is produced because there is twice as much catalyst
No ethanol is produced because too much enzyme denatures the glucose
The rate stays the same because adding yeast has no effect on enzyme concentration
The fermentation finishes faster but the same total amount of ethanol is produced
explanation: More yeast means more enzyme catalyst — the rate increases and the fermentation completes faster. But total ethanol depends on the amount of glucose (unchanged), not the amount of yeast.
hint: Does adding more catalyst change the amount of glucose available to be converted?

prompt: An experiment measures the time for 50 mL of CO₂ to be collected from marble chips reacting with HCl at different concentrations. Results: 0.5 mol/L → 180 s; 1.0 mol/L → 90 s; 2.0 mol/L → 48 s. What conclusion best fits these results?
options: Doubling concentration exactly halves the time taken, so rate is directly proportional to concentration
The results are too variable to draw any conclusion
Concentration has no effect because the mass of marble was not changed
Increasing concentration decreases the time taken, consistent with higher collision frequency increasing rate
explanation: As concentration doubles, time roughly halves (180→90 s) then halves again (though 90→48 s isn't exact halving). The clear trend — more concentration, less time — is consistent with more frequent collisions increasing rate.
hint: What does a shorter time to collect the same volume of gas tell you about the rate?

prompt: A student dissolves catalase (a protein enzyme) in a buffer solution and measures the rate of H₂O₂ decomposition at 10 °C, 37 °C, and 80 °C. She gets rates of: slow, fast, very slow. Which explanation accounts for all three results?
options: At 10 °C the enzyme is too warm; at 37 °C the temperature is optimal; at 80 °C the activation energy is too low
At 10 °C the enzyme is denatured; at 37 °C it is repaired; at 80 °C it decomposes the H₂O₂ directly without a catalyst
Temperature has no effect — the rate differences are all due to pH changes in the buffer
At 10 °C fewer collisions occur and the enzyme is slower; at 37 °C the enzyme is at optimal temperature; at 80 °C the enzyme is denatured and inactive
explanation: At 10 °C, low temperature means fewer collisions with enough energy — slow rate. At 37 °C (body temperature), the enzyme works optimally. At 80 °C, the protein denatures (loses its shape) and loses catalytic activity, giving a very slow rate.
hint: High temperature can both help reactions AND damage protein structure — which effect wins at 80 °C?

prompt: A teacher demonstrates two reactions: Reaction 1 uses an enzyme catalyst; Reaction 2 uses a metal oxide catalyst. A student says both should stop working if heated to 200 °C. Is the student correct?
options: No — heating to 200 °C would speed up both reactions, not stop them
Only for Reaction 2 — metal oxides melt at 200 °C but enzymes are heat-stable
Yes — all catalysts are destroyed at temperatures above 100 °C
Only for Reaction 1 — the enzyme (protein) would be denatured; MnO₂ is unaffected by such temperatures
explanation: Enzymes are proteins that denature at high temperatures (typically above ~50–60 °C), losing their catalytic shape. Inorganic metal oxide catalysts like MnO₂ are not denatured — they are stable at much higher temperatures.
hint: Which type of catalyst is a protein that can be damaged by heat?

prompt: A student wants to design a fair test to compare the effect of temperature on the rate of reaction between zinc and dilute sulfuric acid. Which experimental design is correct?
options: Use 1 g zinc powder at 20 °C with 20 mL of 1 mol/L acid; then 1 g zinc powder at 40 °C with 40 mL of 2 mol/L acid
Use 1 g zinc lump at 20 °C with 20 mL of 1 mol/L acid; then 1 g zinc powder at 40 °C with 20 mL of 1 mol/L acid
Use 1 g zinc powder at 20 °C with 20 mL of 1 mol/L acid; then 1 g zinc powder at 40 °C with 20 mL of 1 mol/L acid
Use 2 g zinc powder at 20 °C with 20 mL of 1 mol/L acid; then 1 g zinc powder at 40 °C with 20 mL of 1 mol/L acid
explanation: A fair test changes only temperature. Same form of zinc (powder), same mass (1 g), same volume and concentration of acid — the only difference is temperature (20 °C vs 40 °C).
hint: Count the number of variables that change in each option — only one should differ.

prompt: A reaction between A and B is carried out in four different conditions. Which set of conditions would give the FASTEST rate?
options: Low temperature, dilute solutions, large solid pieces, no catalyst
High temperature, dilute solutions, large solid pieces, no catalyst
Low temperature, concentrated solutions, powdered solid, catalyst present
High temperature, concentrated solutions, powdered solid, catalyst present
explanation: The fastest rate needs every factor working for it: a high temperature (more energetic collisions), concentrated solutions (more frequent collisions), powdered solid (more surface area) and a catalyst (lower activation energy). Only the set with all four gives the maximum rate.
hint: Which set of conditions maximises collision frequency, collision energy, AND lowers the activation energy threshold?

prompt: A chemist has two identical reactions: both use 0.5 g of iron as a catalyst. Reaction X uses the iron as a fine powder; Reaction Y uses it as a solid block. Both use the same reactants and conditions. Which result is expected?
options: Both reactions have the same rate because the mass of catalyst is identical
Reaction Y is faster because the solid block is denser and more concentrated
Reaction X produces more product because more of the catalyst is in contact with reactants
Reaction X is faster because the iron powder has greater surface area, providing more catalytic sites
explanation: For a solid catalyst, rate depends on the surface area of catalyst exposed to reactants. Iron powder has far more surface area than a block → more catalytic sites → faster rate. (Total product still depends on reactant amounts.)
hint: Surface area matters for solid catalysts too, not just solid reactants — think about where the catalysis happens.

prompt: A student notices that a tiny amount of MnO₂ (0.01 g) can catalyse the complete decomposition of a 100 mL volume of hydrogen peroxide. She argues this means MnO₂ must be getting 'regenerated' during the reaction. Is she correct?
options: No — MnO₂ is a reactant and is consumed; 0.01 g is just a very small amount
Yes — this shows that the MnO₂ is regenerated each catalytic cycle and can act repeatedly, which is the key property of a catalyst
No — MnO₂ is generated fresh from the oxygen produced in the reaction
Yes — but only because MnO₂ is an enzyme that can reproduce itself
explanation: The fact that a tiny mass of MnO₂ can catalyse a large amount of H₂O₂ decomposition demonstrates that MnO₂ is regenerated each cycle — it is not consumed. This is the essential property of a catalyst.
hint: If MnO₂ were consumed, how long would 0.01 g last when catalysing 100 mL of H₂O₂?

prompt: A student investigates the rate of reaction between calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid by measuring mass loss over time. She records 120 g at the start and 116.7 g when bubbling stops. She repeats with warmer acid. Which prediction is correct?
options: The final mass will be lower with warmer acid because more CO₂ escapes
The final mass will be higher with warmer acid because heat prevents gas from escaping
The final mass will be the same (116.7 g) because the same amounts of reactants are used, but mass is lost faster
The rate is unchanged because mass loss only depends on the mass of marble
explanation: Same reactant amounts → same total CO₂ produced → same total mass lost. Warmer acid just makes the reaction faster (steeper mass-loss curve), but the final mass is unchanged.
hint: Warmer acid changes the speed of mass loss, not the final amount of CO₂ released.

prompt: A student increases the pressure in a reaction vessel containing only solid and liquid reactants (no gases). What effect will this have on the reaction rate?
options: Rate increases significantly because more particles are squeezed together
Rate doubles because pressure always doubles collision frequency
Rate is essentially unchanged — solids and liquids are almost incompressible so pressure has negligible effect
Rate decreases because pressure opposes the reaction
explanation: Pressure affects gas-phase reactions by changing the density/concentration of molecules. Solids and liquids are essentially incompressible — increasing pressure has negligible effect on their particle spacing and collision rate.
hint: Does squeezing a solid or a liquid make the particles noticeably closer together?

prompt: Experiment 1: 2.0 g marble chips + 30 mL of 1 mol/L HCl at 25 °C → 0.44 g CO₂ produced. Experiment 2: 2.0 g marble chips + 30 mL of 2 mol/L HCl at 25 °C. How much CO₂ is expected from Experiment 2?
options: 0.88 g, because doubling the concentration doubles the product
0.44 g, because the same mass of marble is the limiting factor
0.22 g, because more concentrated acid reacts more completely
0.44 g only if a catalyst is added
explanation: If marble (2.0 g) is the limiting reactant in both experiments, the amount of CO₂ is determined by the marble, not the acid. More concentrated acid just makes the reaction faster — same CO₂ is produced.
hint: Which reactant is the limiting one in these experiments — the marble or the acid?

prompt: A graph shows two reactions: both start with the same reactants but Reaction A finishes in 30 s and Reaction B finishes in 80 s. Both level off at 60 mL of gas. A student concludes Reaction A 'made more product per second'. Is this conclusion valid?
options: Yes — Reaction A made the same amount in less time, so it made more per second (higher rate)
No — both reactions made the same total product, so both have the same rate
No — Reaction A made more product because it finished faster
Yes — any reaction that finishes faster always produces more product
explanation: Rate is defined as product formed per unit time. Reaction A produces 60 mL in 30 s (avg = 2 mL/s); Reaction B produces 60 mL in 80 s (avg = 0.75 mL/s). So Reaction A has a higher rate, though both make the same total. The conclusion is valid.
hint: Rate = amount of product per unit of time. Can the same total product be made at different rates?

prompt: A researcher tests two enzymes (X and Y) that both catalyse the same reaction. At 37 °C, enzyme X gives a rate of 80 μmol/min and enzyme Y gives 20 μmol/min. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Enzyme X produces four times more product than enzyme Y over the same time period
Enzyme X is a more effective catalyst for this reaction at 37 °C — it converts substrate faster
Enzyme Y must have a higher activation energy than enzyme X
Enzyme X increases the total amount of product formed while enzyme Y does not
explanation: A higher rate (80 vs 20 μmol/min) means enzyme X converts substrate to product faster at 37 °C — it is more effective. Total product still depends on substrate amount (unchanged). We can't directly claim enzyme Y has higher activation energy from this data.
hint: Which enzyme completes the conversion more quickly? Does rate tell you about total product or speed of production?

prompt: Two experiments both use excess hydrochloric acid reacting with 1 g of zinc. Experiment P: zinc powder at 30 °C. Experiment Q: zinc lump at 60 °C. A student says Experiment P will be faster because of the surface area. Which evaluation is most accurate?
options: The student is definitely correct — surface area always has a bigger effect than temperature
The student may be wrong — the higher temperature in Q could more than compensate for the lower surface area
The student is correct — temperature only affects reactions involving gases
Both experiments will have identical rates because the same mass of zinc is used
explanation: Both surface area and temperature affect rate, but their relative impacts depend on the magnitude of each change. A 30 °C temperature increase is significant — it may or may not overcome the rate advantage of powder. We cannot determine the faster experiment without data.
hint: Is surface area always a bigger effect than temperature, or does it depend on how much each factor changes?

prompt: A student collects the following data for the reaction of iron with dilute sulfuric acid. Experiment 1: 1 g iron filings, 30 mL of 1 mol/L H₂SO₄, 25 °C — takes 3 minutes to complete. Experiment 2: 1 g iron filings, 30 mL of 1 mol/L H₂SO₄, 25 °C, with a small piece of copper metal added. Experiment 2 takes 1.5 minutes. What role does the copper play?
options: Copper acts as a reactant and reacts with the iron
Copper acts as a catalyst, speeding up the reaction between iron and the acid
Copper provides additional surface area to the iron filings
Copper increases the concentration of the sulfuric acid
explanation: Copper (in contact with iron in an acid) sets up a galvanic cell that accelerates iron dissolution — the copper acts catalytically (it is not consumed as a primary reactant). Faster completion with unchanged amounts is consistent with catalytic action.
hint: The copper speeds up the reaction but is not consumed — what does that describe?

prompt: A table shows gas volume collected at 1-minute intervals for two reactions: both use 0.5 g Mg + 50 mL 1 mol/L HCl. Reaction 1 at 25 °C; Reaction 2 at 45 °C. At 2 minutes, Reaction 1 shows 80 mL and Reaction 2 shows 160 mL. At 5 minutes, both show 220 mL. What can be concluded?
options: Reaction 2 produced more gas because it was at a higher temperature
Both reactions produced the same total gas because they had the same reactant amounts; Reaction 2 just produced it faster
Reaction 1 produced less gas because lower temperature reduces product yield
Higher temperature in Reaction 2 doubled the amount of Mg that reacted
explanation: Both reactions used the same amounts of Mg and HCl, so the total H₂ produced is the same (220 mL). Reaction 2 (at 45 °C) reached 160 mL by 2 min vs. 80 mL for Reaction 1 — it was faster, not more productive.
hint: Both reactions end at 220 mL — what does this tell you about which factor determines the total gas volume?

prompt: The activation energy for reaction X is 80 kJ/mol. A catalyst reduces this to 50 kJ/mol. A student says this means 37.5% more collisions will now be successful. Why is this reasoning flawed?
options: It is correct — 30 kJ saved out of 80 kJ is exactly 37.5% more successful collisions
The proportion of successful collisions does not scale linearly with the reduction in activation energy — the relationship is exponential, so far more than 37.5% more collisions will be successful
Reducing activation energy has no effect on collision success — only collision frequency matters
The student's maths is wrong — 30/80 is 37.5%, but this should be calculated differently
explanation: The fraction of collisions with energy ≥ Ea follows an exponential (Arrhenius) relationship. Reducing Ea by even a small amount dramatically increases the proportion of successful collisions — the effect is exponential, not linear.
hint: Does the fraction of particles with enough energy to react scale simply with activation energy, or is the relationship more dramatic?

prompt: Which of the following is the best definition of a 'successful collision' in the context of reaction rate?
options: Any collision between two particles of different substances
A collision in which the particles have enough energy (≥ activation energy) AND the correct orientation to react
A collision that produces the maximum possible amount of product
A collision that results in a catalyst being formed
explanation: A successful collision requires both sufficient energy (at least equal to the activation energy) AND the correct geometric orientation of the colliding particles for bonds to break and form. Both conditions must be met.
hint: Even with enough energy, does a head-on vs. glancing collision always work? Think about orientation.

prompt: A student runs four trials of the same reaction, varying one factor in each. Results: Trial 1 (baseline): rate = 1 unit. Trial 2 (double concentration): rate = 2 units. Trial 3 (10 °C higher): rate = 2.1 units. Trial 4 (catalyst added): rate = 3.8 units. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Temperature has no effect because the difference between Trials 2 and 3 is small
All three changes have the same effect on rate
In this reaction, the catalyst has the largest effect on rate of the three changes tested
Doubling concentration is always more effective than increasing temperature
explanation: The data shows: doubling concentration → 2× rate; raising temperature 10 °C → 2.1× rate; catalyst → 3.8× rate. The catalyst has the largest effect among the three changes tested in this specific reaction.
hint: Compare the rates in Trials 2, 3 and 4 against Trial 1 — which change gave the biggest increase?

prompt: A chemistry teacher explains that a catalyst does not change the overall energy released or absorbed in a reaction. A student argues that since the catalyst lowers activation energy, it must reduce the heat released. Which response is correct?
options: The student is correct — less activation energy means less energy released
The teacher is correct — the catalyst only affects the pathway (activation energy), not the overall energy difference between reactants and products
The student is correct — a catalyst always makes exothermic reactions less exothermic
The teacher is correct, but only for endothermic reactions
explanation: The overall energy change (ΔH) of a reaction depends on the difference in energy between reactants and products — this is unchanged by a catalyst. The catalyst only lowers the intermediate energy barrier (activation energy), not the start or finish energy levels.
hint: The activation energy is like a hill on the way from reactants to products. Does lowering the hill change where you started or where you end up?

prompt: A student writes: 'We could make the reaction produce more ammonia in the Haber process by using more iron catalyst.' Identify the error in this reasoning and choose the correct statement.
options: The reasoning is correct — more iron catalyst always produces more ammonia
The error is that more catalyst increases rate but does NOT change the equilibrium yield of ammonia; to get more ammonia, you must use more nitrogen or hydrogen
The error is that iron is not a catalyst — it is a reactant in the Haber process
The reasoning is correct because iron lowers activation energy, which shifts the reaction to make more product
explanation: Catalysts only affect rate — they do NOT change how much product can be formed at equilibrium. To increase the total amount of ammonia produced, you must increase the amount of nitrogen or hydrogen used.
hint: Does a catalyst affect the amount of reactant available, or only how quickly it reacts?

prompt: An energy-profile diagram shows a reaction with and without a catalyst. The catalysed curve differs from the uncatalysed one in that it has…
options: a higher peak (activation energy)
a lower peak (activation energy)
different reactants and products
no reactants at all
explanation: A catalyst lowers the activation energy — the 'hump' on the diagram — so the curve peaks lower; the start and end energies (reactants and products) are unchanged.
hint: The catalyst makes the energy hill SHORTER, but the start and finish heights stay the same.

prompt: A reaction between an acid and excess marble chips produces 50 cm³ of CO₂. Repeated with the SAME acid but powdered marble, the volume of CO₂ produced will be…
options: less than 50 cm³
exactly 50 cm³ — but reached faster
more than 50 cm³
zero
explanation: Powdering changes only the rate; the amount of acid (the limiting reactant) is unchanged, so you still get 50 cm³ — just sooner.
hint: What sets the TOTAL volume — the surface area, or the amount of the limiting reactant?

prompt: Why does the rate of most reactions DECREASE as the reaction proceeds?
options: the temperature always falls
the reactant concentrations fall, so collisions become less frequent
the catalyst always wears out
the products act as catalysts
explanation: As reactants are used up, their concentration drops, so particles collide less often — the rate slows until a reactant runs out.
hint: What happens to the amount of reactant left as time goes on?

prompt: Particle theory explains why even a small temperature rise can have a large effect on rate. The key reason is that a small rise in temperature…
options: doubles the number of particles present
greatly increases the FRACTION of particles with energy above the activation energy
lowers the activation energy
changes the reactants into different substances
explanation: Only collisions with energy ≥ the activation energy react; a modest temperature rise sharply increases how many particles clear that bar (as well as making collisions more frequent).
hint: It's about how many particles can finally 'make it over the hill'.

prompt: In an experiment, doubling the concentration of one reactant roughly doubled the initial rate. This fits the idea that rate depends on…
options: the colour of the solution
how frequently the reacting particles collide
the volume of the flask only
the mass of any catalyst used
explanation: Twice the concentration → roughly twice as many collisions per second → roughly twice the initial rate.
hint: More particles in the same space → collisions happen how much more often?

prompt: Two students run the thiosulfate–acid 'disappearing cross' reaction. Student A's cross disappears in 20 s; student B's in 60 s. Which student's reaction was faster, and which probably used the more concentrated thiosulfate?
options: B was faster; B used the more concentrated solution
A was faster; A used the more concentrated solution
they were equally fast
A was faster; B used the more concentrated solution
explanation: A shorter time = a faster reaction, so A was faster — and a more concentrated solution gives more frequent collisions, so A's was more concentrated.
hint: Less time to obscure the cross = faster; faster usually means more concentrated.

prompt: Adding a catalyst speeds up BOTH the forward and the reverse reaction in a reversible system. This tells you a catalyst changes…
options: the position of equilibrium
how QUICKLY equilibrium is reached, but not where it lies
which products form
the temperature of the system
explanation: Because it lowers the activation energy equally for both directions, a catalyst reaches the same equilibrium faster — it doesn't shift it.
hint: It changes the speed of getting there, not the destination.

prompt: Iron is used as a catalyst in the Haber process, N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. After the process has run, the iron…
options: has all turned into ammonia
is recovered chemically unchanged and can be used again
has been completely used up
has become a reactant
explanation: Catalysts aren't consumed; the iron is recovered unchanged and reused — which is why catalysts are economically valuable.
hint: It's a catalyst — what happens to a catalyst by the end of the reaction?

prompt: Sketching a 'volume of gas vs time' graph for the same reaction at a HIGHER temperature, compared with the original, the new line should be…
options: less steep and end at a lower volume
steeper at the start and reach the same final volume sooner
exactly the same as before
steeper and end at a higher volume
explanation: Higher temperature → faster rate → a steeper line that levels off sooner — but the same amount of reactant means the same final volume.
hint: Faster start, same finishing height — just reached earlier.

prompt: Why is a reaction between two solutions usually faster than the 'same' reaction between a solid and a solution?
options: solutions are always hotter
in a solution the particles are already separated and free to move and collide; in a solid only the surface particles can react
solutions contain more atoms
solids act as catalysts
explanation: Dissolved particles can collide throughout the mixture, whereas a solid can only react where its surface is exposed.
hint: Where on a solid lump can a reaction actually happen?

prompt: A student wants to investigate how surface area affects rate. To make it a FAIR test, which must they keep the same in each run?
options: the surface area of the solid
the mass of solid, and the volume, concentration and temperature of the acid
nothing — change everything at once
the colour of the flask
explanation: Only the variable being tested (surface area / lump size) should change; the mass of solid and all the acid conditions must be kept constant.
hint: Change only the one thing you're testing; keep everything else fixed.

prompt: The reaction between magnesium and dilute acid is exothermic. As it runs in an insulated flask the mixture warms up. This warming…
options: has no effect on the rate
tends to raise the rate, partly offsetting the slowdown caused by the falling acid concentration
drops the rate to zero immediately
depends only on the colour of the flask
explanation: Two effects compete: falling reactant concentration slows it, but the self-heating (exothermic) tends to speed it up — the actual rate is the combination.
hint: An exothermic reaction warms its own mixture — and warmer = faster.

prompt: Balance the marble-chips-and-acid reaction: __ CaCO₃ + __ HCl → __ CaCl₂ + __ H₂O + __ CO₂
explanation: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂ — 1 Ca, 1 C, 3 O, 2 H and 2 Cl on each side. The CO₂ given off is what you'd measure to find the rate.
hint: CaCl₂ needs 2 chlorines → 2 HCl; that also gives the 2 hydrogens for the water; then check the carbon and oxygen.

prompt: Put a gas-volume rate experiment in order:
steps: Set up the flask and gas syringe
Add the reactants and start the timer
Record the gas volume at regular time intervals
Find the rate from the steepest part of the graph
explanation: Rate is found from how quickly the measured gas volume changes, especially at the start.
hint: Measurements need a timer before they can become a graph.

prompt: Put the events on a rate-time graph in order:
steps: The reaction is fastest at the start
The rate slows as reactants are used up
The graph levels off when a reactant runs out
explanation: As reactant particles are consumed, collision frequency falls until no more product forms.
hint: The line is steepest when there are most reactant particles.

prompt: Put the fair-test plan for concentration and rate in order:
steps: Choose the concentration of acid as the variable to change
Keep the temperature, acid volume and solid mass the same
Run each trial and measure the same rate indicator
Use the results to decide how concentration affected rate
explanation: A fair test changes one variable and keeps the other conditions controlled.
hint: Decide what changes, then hold everything else steady.

prompt: Put the collision-theory explanation for higher temperature in order:
steps: Particles gain kinetic energy as temperature rises
Particles move faster through the mixture
Collisions happen more often and with more energy
A larger fraction of collisions exceed the activation energy
explanation: Higher temperature speeds reactions by increasing collision frequency and successful collision energy.
hint: Temperature affects both speed and collision energy.
